stem: A nurse catches a medication-selection error before the medication reaches the client. No harm occurs. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Acknowledge and document the near miss according to the organization's safety-reporting process
options.B: Avoid reporting it because the client was not harmed
options.C: Report it only if the same error occurs again and reaches a client
options.D: Delete any record of the event because near misses are not safety events

rationale: The 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan includes acknowledging and documenting practice errors and near misses within Safety and Infection Prevention and Control. A near miss remains safety-relevant even when it is intercepted before reaching the client. Therefore A is the best action. Lack of injury does not eliminate the need to follow the organization's safety-reporting process.
educational_objective: Recognize and report near misses according to organizational safety processes even when no client harm occurs.
source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
source_locator: Detailed Test Plan, Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — Related Activity Statements from the 2024 RN Practice Analysis, printed p.24 / PDF p.28: acknowledge and document practice errors and near misses
source_claim_supported: Entry-level RNs should acknowledge and document practice errors and near misses as part of safety practice.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — acknowledge and document practice errors and near misses, printed p.24 / PDF p.28

correction_summary: Replaced the source item's non-universal inference that a stronger safety culture necessarily produces higher overall voluntary reporting rates. The revised item directly tests the NCSBN 2026 entry-level nursing activity of acknowledging and documenting near misses. Blueprint corrected from Management of Care to Safety and Infection Prevention and Control.
audit_findings: A directly matches the NCSBN activity statement. B, C, and D incorrectly treat absence of harm as a reason not to report a near miss. The item avoids claiming a specific event-reporting form, punitive model, or facility-wide reporting-rate relationship. One best answer and direct NCLEX relevance remain.
